sentences.text: Aristonectes is an extinct genus of plesiosaur from the Late Cretaceous of what is now South America and Antarctica, a group historically difficult to analyze due to the incompleteness of its fossil remains.
The genus measured more than 10 meters in length, with one referred specimen from Antarctica estimated to be over 11 meters long.
The skulls of both known species are flattened and ogive-shaped, while the best-preserved swim paddle of Aristonectes quiriquinensis is about 3 meters long, indicating a total wingspan of 7 meters.
The holotype specimen was interpreted as an adult or elderly individual, and its specific name parvidens means "small teeth," referring to the small size of the tooth sockets.
Over 793 gastroliths were found in the largest known specimen of Aristonectes, MLP 89-III-3-1, from Antarctica.
The long limbs of Aristonectes are comparable in proportion to the Early Jurassic rhomaleosaurid Meyerasaurus and the modern humpback whale.
The curved cervical ribs and neural spines likely allowed the animal to maintain its trunk higher than its head.
The genus Aristonectes was described by Ángel Cabrera in 1941, and the type species Aristonectes parvidens was originally named by him that same year.
Cabrera described Aristonectes parvidens in 1941 based on a specimen from Chubut Province, Argentina.

The holotype specimen of Aristonectes quiriquinensis (SGO.PV.260) was found in Maastrichtian beds of the Quiriquina Formation, and two additional specimens from Quiriquina Island were referred to Aristonectes quiriquinensis in 2015.
A referred specimen of Aristonectes was discovered in the López de Bertodano Formation in Antarctica.
Based on its cranial morphology and fossil evidence, Aristonectes likely fed by mixing prey and sediment in benthic zones.

It is hypothesized that Aristonectes used gastroliths to aid digestion or reduce buoyancy, though the latter is poorly supported, and O'Gorman and colleagues concluded in 2014 that Aristonectes swallowed random batches of sediment containing stones rather than selecting individual gastroliths.
Based on fossil distribution, Aristonectes likely regularly migrated between Patagonia and Antarctica.

Cabrera classified Aristonectes within the family Elasmosauridae in 1941 based on cranial element shape, and Ketchum and Benson recovered Aristonectes parvidens as an elasmosaurid in 2010, supporting the earlier classification by Gasparini et al. (2003).
Recent research on Aristonectes parvidens and A. quiriquinensis allowed scientists to classify the genus among the elasmosaurids, and Aristonectes belongs to the subfamily Aristonectinae.
Aristonectes lived during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, and Aristonectes quiriquinensis lived during the Maastrichtian stage.
Aristonectes lived from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian stages, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.
It is debated whether the holotype of Plesiosaurus chilensis belongs to A. parvidens, with some researchers suggesting it does.
It is likely that Aristonectes quiriquinensis had fewer teeth than A. parvidens, based on the preservation of tooth sockets.
Samuel P. Welles considered Aristonectes to be an indeterminate pliosaur in 1962 due to its enigmatic anatomy.
O'Keefe and colleagues expressed skepticism in 2011 about grouping Aristonectes and Kaiwhekea with Tatenectes due to morphological discrepancies.
It is debated whether mosasaurs in the López de Bertodano Formation attacked contemporary plesiosaurs like Aristonectes.
